content.title: Thank you for your valuable comments
content.comment:
Thank you to the reviewer for mentioning that our proposed method leads to good performance on image, text, and graph datasets. Please find our detailed responses below, which we hope can address the reviewer's concerns:

**P2**: Gradient-based uncertainty in [1] has been found to be robust to model architecture, batch size, etc. Then, we adopt the concept of gradient similarity, where prior work has shown that gradient similarity is equivalent to the influence function of a training data point on test inputs. Here, we use the same concept to compute the influence of  $x_j$ on the loss w.r.t $x_i$ [2]. That means, the uncertainty score assigns higher scores for the negative examples that are more influential for the corresponding anchor. We have revised the uncertainty description in the updated paper version. 

 **False negative**: As mentioned in Appendix E (limitation), from our experimental analysis we verify that the probability of false negative examples arriving in a given batch decreases as the number of classes increases. Hence, feature similarity can still perform well in these cases. Nevertheless, from the results, we observe that when false negative examples are sampled, they can significantly hamper the learning process. Also note that compared to HCL in Table 1, which performs augmentation in the feature space, the feature similarity reported in Table 2 is with augmentations in the image space. UnMix in particular has shown that Mixup in the image space performs better over strong baselines. Thus, this change in augmentations used also contributes to the final performance.

**Un-Mix for Table 4 and Figure 5**: As UnMix is specifically designed for image domains, it's not possible to use UnMix as a baseline for sentence representations (Table 4). UnMix works by mixing images at pixel level by using MixUp. As for Fig. 5, due to this interpolation, the UnMix images become complex and hard to interpret. We suspect that this might be the reason why the UnMix work does not provide any qualitative examples in their paper. Our revised supplementary material now includes two additional comparisons with UnMix: (1) on ImageNet and (2) in transfer learning settings.

**Advantage of learning weights**:  Using equal weights will assign the same weight to the components while training for different datasets and may not result in optimal performance. However, the attention-based module that aggregates the three components can learn to assign more attention to the components that are more important for a particular dataset. While we perform analysis of both, showing some improvements with the use of attention, we note that attention-based interpolation is not the main focus of our work, but rather motivating and experimentally validating the integration of the three proposed components (uncertainty, diversity, and similarity).


**Performance of graph datasets is not competitive**: For graphs, we suspect that the datasets are less diverse and that's why we did not get significant improvement. We have included these results and our explanation, as we believe that showing cases/domains where the proposed method may not work well is equally important. Nevertheless, we have also demonstrated improvements in several text classification and image representation learning tasks.  

[1] Jordan T Ash, Chicheng Zhang, Akshay Krishnamurthy, John Langford, and Alekh Agarwal. Deep batch active learning by diverse, uncertain gradient lower bounds. In ICLR, 2020.

[2] Dhaliwal, Jasjeet, and Saurabh Shintre. "Gradient similarity: An explainable approach to detect adversarial attacks against deep learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:1806.10707 (2018).

content.title: Thank you for the response
content.comment:
Thank you very much for responding to our rebuttal and for increasing the rating of our work! Please find our clarifications below, which we hope are addressing some of the expressed concerns. 

**P2**: As we don't have the label information, we create a pseudo-label space (updated in the paper). This pseudo-label space will create a decision boundary. Note that the use of pseudo-labels in self-supervised learning (and their corresponding formed decision boundaries) is not new; for example, [1,2,3] have similar approaches, where [1] uses pseudo-labeling to calculate gradients, [2] uses clustering to form pseudo-labels, [3] uses the pseudo-labels from a teacher network trained in a self-supervised fashion to train a student network. Given this pseudo-label space and the corresponding decision boundary, UnDiMix will assign more importance to the examples that have the most influence on the anchor. The higher the gradient norm of the negative example, the higher the uncertainty for this example is, i.e., the closer the example is to the decision boundary created by the pseudo-label space. The higher the gradient similarity between the anchor and the negative example is, the more influence the negative example will have during training.


**Contribution of each component**: Thank you for the discussion. We have now performed additional experiments with variants of the attention weights: 1) **Constrained** where the attention weights form a probability distribution, \ie $0\leq w_u, w_s, w_r \leq 1$ and $w_u + w_s + w_r = 1$ where $w_u$, $w_s$ and $w_r$ are the attention weights of uncertainty, similarity and diversity components, respectively 2) **Unconstrained** where there are no constraints for the attention weights. The following [link](https://www.dropbox.com/s/da11gm91lcfdp0s/Hard_Negative_Selections_in_Contrastive_Learning.pdf?dl=0) contains the trends of attention weights over 400 epochs (Figure 10 in supplementary material). We can see that the constrained attention module can learn to assign more attention to the components that are more important for a particular dataset. 


**Diversity of graph datasets:** Please find below the dataset summary for the graph datasets
| Dataset     | PROTEINS | PTC   | IMDB-M | IMDB-B | ENZYMES | MUTAG |
|-------------|----------|-------|--------|--------|---------|-------|
| No. graphs  | 1113     | 344   | 1500   | 1000   | 600     | 188   |
| No. classes | 2        | 2     | 3      | 2      | 6       | 2     |
| Avg. nodes  | 39.06    | 14.29 | 13     | 19.77  | 32.63   | 17.93 |
| Avg. edges  | 72.82    | 14.69 | 65.94  | 96.53  | 62.14   | 19.79 |

Here, we can see that the number of classes varies between 2-6 for all datasets. Given these datasets and the evidence provided in the experiments in our paper (e.g Figure 1), we kindly ask the reviewer to further elaborate on what other type of evidence we could provide, if needed, e.g., suggest additional experiments we could potentially try.

[1] Ma, Shuang, et al. "Active Contrastive Learning of Audio-Visual Video Representations." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2020.

[2] Caron, Mathilde, et al. "Unsupervised learning of visual features by contrasting cluster assignments." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (2020): 9912-9924.

[3] Petrovai, Andra, and Sergiu Nedevschi. "Exploiting Pseudo Labels in a Self-Supervised Learning Framework for Improved Monocular Depth Estimation." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2022.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposed a new approach to the mining of hard negatives during contrastive learning.
It argues for a combination of three properties to make sampling of hard negatives more reasonable.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- Numerous datasets and numerous modalities are considered making the considered benchmark a strong one (while there are some issues, see below)

Weakness:
- Comparison of Table 4 in [3] and Table 2 in this article [*] makes me sad. E.g. for SUBJ in [3] Hard gives accuracy 87, QT gives 86; in [*] UnDiMix gives 86.8, QT gives 79.9. (1) it is strange that the results for QT degraded so much. (2) Hard is better than UnDiMix. I compared the results from these articles and from the article that introduced this protocol [4]. The article [4] presents the best results. See Table I composed at https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1BJRFzDsSn8ik5Bf7Fcue7KuMxXFTmvMn02ac0EFTkUE/edit?usp=sharing for the comparison of results in different articles. The paper [4] has the official GitHub implementation available [5]. 
- The most important questions that the paper doesn't answer is why there are only three options considered: "Uncertainty, feature similarity, and diversity". Maybe, we don't need some of them, or we miss something important? 
- Selection of a particular uncertainty measure seems unjustified. The norm of the gradient function is OK to some extent to capture part of the uncertainty, while there is no justification for why the scalar product of this gradient is relevant to the uncertainty for a particular pair of objects. If so, it can help in other open-set classification problems as well, where uncertainty estimation of a pair of objects remains a hard problem with complex approaches developed [1] or natural heuristics with theoretical justification developed [2]
- Diversity measure also seems weakly justified. Is it possible to provide some theoretical and empirical justifications that this measure is fine?
- Results from Table 2 for CIFAR-100 look strange: there 1.5 per cent improvement c.t. other options. Can you explain the behaviour behind it?

1. Shi, Yichun, and Anil K. Jain. "Probabilistic face embeddings." ICCV. 2019.

3. Robinson, Joshua David, et al. "Contrastive Learning with Hard Negative Samples." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2020.
4. Logeswaran, Lajanugen, and Honglak Lee. "An efficient framework for learning sentence representations." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2018.
5. https://github.com/lajanugen/S2V

content.title: Thank you for your valuable comments
content.comment:
Thank you to the reviewer for mentioning that numerous datasets and numerous modalities are considered in our paper, making the considered benchmark a strong one. Please find our detailed responses below, which we hope that they adequately address the reviewer's concerns:


**Results of sentence representation**: Thank you for your concerns. HCL provided an algorithm in their paper which uses NT-Xent loss whereas the official implementation of [5] used Cross-Entropy (CE) loss. To have a fair comparison between the baselines we used the same loss function across all baselines, i.e., the NT-Xent loss mentioned in the HCL [3]. We reported results for that. As HCL [3] did not provide any code for this variation, we have no way to verify our implementation of HCL [3]. Note that HCL does not provide code for the sentence representation tasks. We are now working on the implementation of HCL using CE, which will also be mainly based on our intuition. Moreover, the BookCorpus dataset now holds less data than before, as several articles became private. We suspect that this affects the result and that is why the results are different from the tables in the previous papers.

 **Why only uncertainty, feature similarity, and diversity**: From our extensive literature review and experimental analysis, we found these three components are useful for selecting hard negative examples. We have provided intuitive explanations for all 3 properties. We agree that for some datasets and tasks, some of the components may not be necessary. That is why we created an attention-based module to aggregate these three components, where the attention-based interpolation will leave out a component if it's not necessary or contributing enough for a given dataset.

**Selection of uncertainty measure**: Thank you for the references! Gradient-based uncertainty in [1] has been found to be robust to model architecture, batch size, etc. Then, we adopt the concept of gradient similarity, where prior work has shown that gradient similarity is equivalent to the influence function of a training data point on test inputs. Here, we use the same concept to compute the influence of  $x_j$ on the loss w.r.t $x_i$ [2]. That means, the uncertainty score assigns higher scores for the negative examples that are more influential for the corresponding anchor. We have revised the uncertainty measure description in the updated paper version.

 **Diversity measure**: The diversity measure we propose calculates the average distance from all other negative examples. Thus, the negative examples which are farther away from other negative examples will have higher scores and the negative examples which are closer to each other will have lower scores. In that way, this measure incorporates diversity while selecting negative examples. While this is an approximation of diversity, our experiments in Fig. 8 show that this is computationally much more efficient than clustering. In our preliminary experiments, we made use of clustering instead of the proposed diversity measure and have observed that results were negative, with the clustering variant of UnDiMix underperforming (not reported in the paper, but we can include it if needed) 

**Table 2 results:** We kindly ask the reviewer to further explain this question. This table presents an ablation analysis of each proposed component, or combinations thereof.

**Equation (2) confusion**: Apologies for the confusion. We have revised the notation in the updated version by adding $i \in [1,2, \ldots, N]$ in Equation (2)

**Algorithm 1**: Thank you for the improvement suggestions. We tried to cover all metrics and add as many pseudo-comments as possible, and have considered further polishing the pseudocode such as standardizing the font size for the loss update, the similarity metric, etc. in our revised paper version. Nevertheless, we will release the code upon acceptance to make it possible to reproduce our results.

[1] Jordan T Ash, Chicheng Zhang, Akshay Krishnamurthy, John Langford, and Alekh Agarwal. Deep batch active learning by diverse, uncertain gradient lower bounds. In ICLR, 2020.

[2] Dhaliwal, Jasjeet, and Saurabh Shintre. "Gradient similarity: An explainable approach to detect adversarial attacks against deep learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:1806.10707 (2018).

content.summary_of_the_paper:
- The paper proposes strategies to weigh the negatives in a contrastive learning framework. 
- The key idea is to weigh the negatives based on three scores : anchor vicinity, decision boundary vicinity and diversity. The weighing is automatically determined as the learning progresses. 
- The approach leads to good improvements on linear evaluation for various image, graph and language benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper proposes a solution for an important problem of determining which negative samples to focus on for contrastive learning. 
- The paper breaks down the problem into three key requirements for the sampling strategy and proposes objectives which can optimize for each. I like this breakdown.
- The idea is simple but effective as seen by the improvements on various benchmarks. 
- The experimental section is extensive for the tasks and datasets considered. 

Weaknesses:
- While the approach leads to good improvements on linear evaluation on small datasets like CIFAR-10/100, Tiny-ImageNet, these improvements might not hold for larger datasets. I did notice that the authors experimented on IN-1K but at 50 epochs. While the improvements are fair, in my experience the results at 50/100 epochs do not always hold at 200 epochs (where models are usually evaluated). I suggest that the authors atleast train their models for 100 epochs where a couple of published numbers exist (MoCHI, MMCL, etc) and on ImageNet-100. 
- One of the key motivations behind self-supervised learning is transferring the pre-trained models to various downstream tasks. The paper does not evaluate on benchmark transfer learning tasks. I think that is important. 
- From the introduction, "...rarely consider distance from the decision boundary" -- It looks like MMCL explicitly formulates this aspect. Please include a small discussion on this.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The paper is well written and easy to follow
- The proposed approach is interesting, the experiments (while on small datasets) are extensive. The approach is well validated. 
- Novelty : While some of the individual techniques do exist in the literature, the paper combines them in a novel way. 
- Reproduciblity : I do not see any issues if the code is released.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I like the premise of the paper. The approach is simple and easy to implement and comes with little overhead. 
My main concern is that it is unclear if this approach would work as expected with larger datasets where there might fewer false negatives. A fair comparison with previous works on larger datasets and some empirical results on transfer learning would be helpful.

(2021) formulated the contrastive loss function as an SVM objective and utilized the support vectors as hard negatives, resorting to approximations to solve a computationally expensive quadratic equation for each anchor." where Shah et al. (2021) is the MMCL work. MMCL utilizes the support vectors as negative examples excluding other examples, whereas we include other examples as negatives and assign high importance based on the proposed combination of the three scoring metrics.

replying_to: Replying to Thanks for the rebuttal

content.title: Thank you for the response
content.comment:
Thank you for taking the time to read our rebuttal and respond! Please find our clarifications below, we will be happy to provide further details.

**Protocol followed for "Larger dataset results"**: The first difference between our results of Imagenet with previous papers is that we used the FFCV data loader [1] for accelerating training. Secondly, due to resource constraints, we use a batch size of 256 instead of 512. All other training details were kept the same as MoCo-V2 [2]. Note that UnMix training details are different from MoCo-V2; UnMix sets the dimension of the hidden layer of the projection head as 1024 whereas in MoCo-V2 the dimension was kept at 128. In summary, our differences with UnMix are in terms of batch size (256 vs. 512) and projection head dimensionality (128 vs. 1024). Moreover, we trained all our models in a single GPU instead of multiple GPUs (as mentioned in [2]).

**Protocol followed for "Transfer Learning"**: Thank you for sharing this reference. The results reported in [3] are for models trained for 5000 epochs whereas our results are reported with models trained for 1000 epochs. Moreover, as we used the pre-trained model on ImageNet, the difference in training hyperparameters between our implementations and previous papers may affect the results of transfer learning too. Nevertheless, we note that for a fair comparison, we have kept the same settings across all baselines. 

[1] Guillaume Leclerc, Andrew Ilyas, Logan Engstrom, Sung Min Park, Hadi Salman, and Aleksander Madry. FFCV: an optimized data pipeline for accelerating ML training. https://github.com/libffcv/ffcv/, 2022 

[2] https://github.com/facebookresearch/moco

[3] How Well Do Self-Supervised Models Transfer? - CVPR 2021

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper designs a hard negative sampling strategy called UnDiMix, that takes into account anchor similarity, model uncertainty and diversity. The authors argue that a good negative sample for contrastive learning should fulfill the following three characteristics: 1) resembling the anchor example, 2) close to the decision boundary, and 3) semantically similar but with diversity. The proposed UnDiMix utilizes uncertainty to penalize false hard negatives and pairwise distance among negatives to select diverse examples in a computationally inexpensive way. The effectiveness of the UnDiMix is verified by showing the improvements in downstream task performance and negative selection quality on several benchmarks in 3 domains (image, text and graph data).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. This paper tackles an important research problem, as the quality of negative samples in contrastive learning has a significant impact on performance.
2. The idea of considering anchor similarity, model uncertainty and diversity altogether in designing sampling strategies is reasonable and interesting.
3. Empirical results on various benchmarks indeed demonstrate the superiority of the UnDiMix over competitive baselines. 
4. The paper is well-written and easy to follow.


Weaknesses:
1. The paper does not provide enough supporting evidence, both theoretically and empirically, on the rationality behind the design of increasing the diversity of negative samples. According to Figure 1, the diversity is barely measured by the number of negative samples, which is less convincing. Moreover, the authors have stated that they empirically observed that incorporating diversity could improve downstream performance, while I cannot find this part in the paper.
2. Details of the uncertainty-based sampling strategy require further clarification.
   - Why $\hat{y}_j$ in Eq. (3) is maximized over $N$ examples in the batch? What does this pseudo-label mean?
   - The uncertainty score of an example $u(\tilde{x}_j, \bar{x}_i)$ considers uncertainty of the anchor $x_i$, why?
3. The authors claim that their proposed diversity score (in Eq. (4)) adds little to no computational overhead, which should be analyzed and derived rigorously.
4. Some
uncertainty-based sampling strategies (like Ma et al., 2021) should also be
compared in experiments.
5. Most experiments and analyses are conducted on the image domain, while the performance improvements on the other two domains are not significant.
6. Some symbols are misused. Like $\chi_{N}$, which is the set of sample pairs but also used to represent the set negative samples ($ \tilde{x}_{j\neq i} \in \chi_N$).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Although the paper is generally well-written, there still exists room for improving clarity. For example,
- If the “empirical analysis” claimed in the contributions refers to “Qualitative Analysis” in Sec. 4.1, then it should be moved to before the methodology part.

The novelty is somewhat limited since the designed strategy is based on an aggregated metric considering anchor similarity, model uncertainty and diversity, all of which are independently adopted in existing works.

As for reproducibility, the authors claim to provide the source code after acceptance.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given the listed weaknesses and other comments on clarity and novelty, I think this is a borderline paper.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

display_title: Thank you for your valuable comments

content.title: Thank you for your valuable comments
content.comment:
Thank you to the reviewer for mentioning that our paper tackles an important research problem and that the idea of considering anchor similarity, model uncertainty, and diversity altogether in designing sampling strategies is reasonable and interesting. Also thank you for stating that empirical results on various benchmarks indeed demonstrate the superiority of the UnDiMix over competitive baselines and that our paper is well-written and easy to follow.


Please find our detailed  responses to your comments below:

**Rationality behind the design of increasing the diversity of negative samples**: In figure 1, the number of negative samples is the same for each experiment, that is (2 x batch_size) - 2, removing the anchor and positive example from the batch. However, when sampling these (2 x batch_size) - 2 negative samples we restricted the sampling to k classes. Therefore, when k is small the diversity of the negative examples is low and vice versa. By doing this experiment we demonstrate that the diversity of the negative examples is necessary for improving the performance of the learning task. In Table 2, we observe that diversity alone achieves good performance, comparable to uncertainty and that incorporating both uncertainty and diversity (the main focus of this work) results in performance improvements across all datasets. Moreover, in supplementary Fig. 8, we show that the proposed diversity scoring function is computationally less expensive than clustering.

**Meaning of pseudo-label and uncertainty of anchor in uncertainty score**: We adopt the concept of pseudo-label from [1] (Ma et.al., 2021). Generally, a pseudo-label is defined as the label predicted by the model. In our method, we define a pseudo-label space induced by the anchors and take the gradient of the last layer of the encoder with respect to the most confident pseudo-label prediction. Due to the absence of class information, we design an auxiliary pseudo-labeling task of predicting the corresponding augmented example $\bar{x}_j$ given its pair $\tilde{x}_j$. We denote the most confident prediction as $\hat{y}_j = \arg\max_k[{y}_j = \bar{x}_k| \tilde{x}_j, \mathcal{X}_N]_k$, where $[\cdot]_k$ corresponds to the index of example $x_i$ in the batch and $1\leq k\leq N$. That is, given the augmented view $\tilde{x}_i$ of example $x_i$, the goal is to locate the matching augmented example $\bar{x}_i$ from the set of augmented views $\bar{x}_1, \bar{x}_2, \ldots, \bar{x}_k, \ldots, \bar{x}_N$ for all examples in the batch. We have revised this description in the updated paper version. 

The gradient of the loss function w.r.t each data point is a measure of model uncertainty, termed gradient-based uncertainty in [2], which has been found to be robust to model architecture, batch size, etc. In Equation (3), if the gradient is high that means the model is not confident about its prediction which makes the negative example hard. Then, we adopt the concept of gradient similarity, where prior work has shown that gradient similarity is equivalent to the influence function of a training data point on test inputs. Here, we use the same concept to compute the influence of  $x_j$ on the loss w.r.t $x_i$ [3]. That means, the uncertainty score assigns higher scores for the negative examples that are more influential for the corresponding anchor. We have revised this description in the updated paper version.

**Computational overhead**: We included an analysis of the computational overhead in Appendix C. Specifically, we compared the minutes required per epoch for HCL, UnDiMix, and the clustering-based approach SWAV. We can see that UnDiMix takes a similar time as HCL even after taking diversity into account, whereas SWAV takes much more time to complete one epoch.

**Ma et.al., 2021 baseline**: Ma et.al., 2021 was originally built for cross-modal learning of video and corresponding audio. Although they mentioned their code is present in [1], we found the code unreproducible. Firstly, there are no instructions on which file to run to train and the hyperparameters. Secondly, their shared implementation of the k-means algorithm is very inefficient and the code takes forever to do clustering in a single epoch. We are working towards (1) making their implementation efficient and this possible to run in a reasonable time, and (2) adapting it for a single modality, but both require sufficient effort on our end. If we finish these in time, we will share the results, otherwise, we will be happy to include results in the camera-ready version.

[1] https://github.com/yunyikristy/CM-ACC

[2] Jordan T Ash, Chicheng Zhang, Akshay Krishnamurthy, John Langford, and Alekh Agarwal. Deep batch active learning by diverse, uncertain gradient lower bounds. In ICLR, 2020.

[3] Dhaliwal, Jasjeet, and Saurabh Shintre. "Gradient similarity: An explainable approach to detect adversarial attacks against deep learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:1806.10707 (2018).

content.title: Continued Response
content.comment:
**Improvements on the other two domains are not significant**: For graphs, we suspect that the datasets are less diverse and that's why we did not get significant improvement. However, for sentence representation, our model performs better than the baselines in 6 of the 7 downstream tasks. Table 4 covers 7 text classification tasks, and shows that UnDiMix achieves up to 16.8% relative gains over the next best strategy (10-fold cross-validation).

**Misuse of symbols**: Apologies for the notation misuse. The set of negative samples will be  $(\bar{x}_j, \tilde{x}_j) \in \mathcal{X}_N$. We fixed it in the updated version

**Novelty**: Our work aims to introduce an efficient self-supervised method. To calculate the diversity score of negative examples, we propose a metric based on pairwise similarity, whereas previous methods (such as SWAV) used clustering to incorporate diversity. Yet, we find that clustering-based methods are computationally expensive to run in each epoch. To the best of our knowledge, no existing work has jointly considered anchor similarity, uncertainty (influence), and diversity in hard negative mining for self-supervised contrastive learning. Our work provides an extensive qualitative and quantitative analysis to evaluate the contribution of each component.
